title: Arbor: Locating Reasoning Failures in Long Chains of Thought through Reasoning State Tracking

paper.title: Arbor : Locating Reasoning Failures in Long Chains of Thought through Reasoning State Tracking
paper.abstract:
Abstract Large reasoning models solve complex problems through long chains of thought, in which prior work has documented failure modes such as overthinking, underthinking, and unsupported deductions. Existing methods detect these failures from local signals: textual similarity to nearby steps, switch tokens, or an LLM’s judgment of a step’s correctness. However, what a step contributes to the solution depends on the state that earlier steps have established, so identifying failures requires a global view that tracks that state across the trajectory. Therefore, we propose Arbor , a reasoning-failure attribution framework that represents each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states , built as each step creates, verifies, prunes, or revisits a state, and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and the state preceding it. Using Arbor , we refine the three failure modes into distinct subtypes that harm reasoning through different mechanisms and at different costs. We find that the tree state Arbor maintains before a step separates failure steps from the at-risk steps at which the failure did not occur. We discuss how Arbor integrates with existing mitigations at inference time and in training data.
Code, data and interactive examples are available at https://inklab.usc.edu/ARBOR .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large reasoning models (LRMs) solve complex reasoning tasks with long chains of thought (CoT) in which they derive intermediate results, verify them, backtrack and pivot to alternatives. Prior work has documented recurring failure modes in these trajectories: overthinking, in which the model re-reasons about results it has already established ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Pipis et al., 2026 ) ; underthinking, in which it abandons a line of reasoning that could still succeed, a premature switch as opposed to a justified switch away from a line already ruled out ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ; and unsupported deductions, steps the preceding context does not entail ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ) . These failures waste inference budget and some produce wrong answers; reducing them requires knowing which steps fail and why . Existing methods detect these failures with signals that are local to a step: recurring n n -grams or embedding similarity between nearby sentences for repetition ( Pipis et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zhen et al., 2025 ) , thought-switch tokens such as alternatively for underthinking ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , process reward models and LLM judges for step correctness ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and block-level functional labels spanning many steps ( Marjanović et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025b ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Bogdan et al., 2025 ) . None conditions a step’s label on which earlier steps it depends on and what they established, although that context is what makes a derivation a repetition, a switch premature or a deduction unsupported (related work in Appendix A ). Figure 1: How a step relates to the states already established defines a reasoning failure. (a) An excerpt of a Qwen3-8B trajectory on a ZebraLogic puzzle; numbers are step indices, and colored steps are labeled by function. (b) Its tree of reasoning states: nodes are intermediate states, tagged with the steps that created or revisited them, edges link each state to the states derived from it, and the case split at step 66 opens two branches. Steps 87–88 are a repetition : they re-derive the state of step 68 in new words. Step 86 is underthinking : it abandons Case 2 while that branch is still viable. Step 90 is an unsupported deduction : it contradicts the Case 1 assumption. Step 113 is a justified switch : it follows the pruning of Case 1 at step 112. Figure 2: Local signals miss or misattribute the failures that the reasoning state identifies. Columns are steps of the trajectory in Figure 1 . For each failure mode, local signals (gray, dotted) are compared with Arbor (colored, solid), whose arrow points to the earlier step whose state determines the label. Repetition: step 88 shares no n n -gram with step 68, and embedding similarity links it to the clue recap at step 53 rather than to the state it re-derives. Underthinking: a switch token fires at both step 86 and step 113, but only step 86 leaves a viable branch. Unsupported deduction: the process reward model misses step 90, which violates the Case 1 assumption of step 66, and flags the correct retraction at step 112 instead. We therefore define reasoning failures relative to the state of the reasoning , the intermediate results established, the branches open and the constraints in force when a step occurs. We represent each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states (Figure 1 ), in which nodes are intermediate results, each edge records the node a step derives from, and where a step attaches identifies a failure; Figure 2 shows why local signals fail on the same trajectory. We make these relations explicit with Arbor ( A ttributing R easoning failures B y O perations on R easoning-state trees), a pipeline in three stages (Figure 3 ; § 2 ): an LLM parses each step into an operation on a canonical, wording-invariant payload; a deterministic engine resolves the step against the tree built so far and applies the corresponding mutation; and we define failures as relations between a step and a specific earlier state, which refines the three failure modes into distinct subtypes (Table 1 ). We instantiate the framework on three reasoning tasks with distinct reasoning structures, constraint satisfaction (ZebraLogic; Lin et al., 2025 ), search over arithmetic compositions (24 Game 1 1 1 nlile/24-game ) and sequential action planning under preconditions (PlanBench; Valmeekam et al., 2023 ), and report three findings. First, Arbor flags failures more accurately than local signals (§ 4 ). The local signals recover only a small share of the steps Arbor flags, and what they flag instead is mostly ordinary reasoning. Arbor ’s per-subtype counts separate incorrect from correct trajectories better than all local signals combined. Second, the distinct subtypes of each failure mode differ in cost and mechanism (§ 5 ). Unsupported deduction costs correctness, since the model’s verification seldom catches a step the state does not support, and the step enters the answer. Underthinking costs the search expended before the model reaches the answer by another path or by returning to the branch, rather than correctness, since it usually still reaches it. Repetition does the least harm to the answer and costs few tokens beyond its own steps, since the model re-establishes a step it proposed long before and gains nothing from it. Within each mode, the subtypes differ in which of these costs they carry. Third, the tree state before a step separates each modeled subtype from the at-risk steps at which it did not end up occurring (§ 6 ). The precursor of each modeled subtype is the content of the branch, whether the current node has been verified, or the recent operations. Operation labels alone recover only the last kind, and the first two precede the subtypes that cost correctness or viable work, which therefore require the tree. To our knowledge, Arbor is the first reasoning-failure attribution framework that maintains the solution state of a reasoning trajectory step by step and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and that state, rather than to the step’s text. Tracking the state enables us to separate the subtypes of a failure mode, measure what each costs in tokens and in correctness, and identify the state that precedes a failure. We discuss how Arbor integrates with existing mitigation at inference time and in training data (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: 2 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 3: Arbor ’s three-stage framework. Each row is one relation between a step and the results the model has established before it; § 2.3 gives the predicate on the reasoning-state tree. A row is undefined, rather than approximated, on a task whose structure has no state for it (Appendix H ). Arbor (Attributing Reasoning failures By Operations on Reasoning-state trees) turns a trajectory x 1 , … , x T x_{1},\dots,x_{T} into a tree of reasoning states in three stages (Figure 3 ): a parser maps each step to an operation on a schema-grounded payload; a deterministic engine resolves the step to a node of the tree built so far and applies one mutation; and a failure row (Table 1 ) is a predicate on the step, the node it resolves to and the tree before it. Only the parser calls a model; the same parse always replays to the same tree and the same labels, and every label names the earlier node it is defined against.

A result is a fact, value, action or subgoal. The first stage, the parser, assigns every step one of seven operations (Table 2 ) together with its payload , the schema-grounded content the operation acts on: a fact, value, action, subgoal, hypothesis or answer. Derive adds a result, Assume opens a branch, Verify records a verdict on a result, Prune closes a branch, Confirm commits an answer, Restate repeats a result without deriving it, and Meta carries no content. For each task we customize the parser’s prompt with a puzzle schema , the entities, the allowed predicates, the allowed operations with their preconditions and effects, the initial state and the goal, and the parser outputs in that schema, so “Bob lives in the fifth house” and “house 5’s name is Bob” parse to the same atom. We use Qwen3.8-27B as the parser; it sees the puzzle schema, the current step, its labeled neighborhood and the schema elements of the previous steps. The parser reaches an accuracy of 0.89 or above on adjudicated reference labels on every task (Appendix E ). The parser thus records only what each step does, in isolation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Engine
sections.text: From these per-step operations the engine builds the tree of reasoning states, applying each step to the tree built from the steps before it.

sections.heading: Tree.
sections.text: A node v v holds an intermediate result or hypothesis (a cell assignment, a value composed from a subset of the tiles, a world state after an action) together with the solution state s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) reached at it: the board with every cell placed so far, the tiles still unused, the facts that hold after the actions taken. The lineage of v v is the path from the root to v v . A branch is the subtree below a hypothesis. A node’s status is open, closed by the model, contradictory as detected by the engine, or committed. The frontier is the set of open leaves, and the current leaf is the frontier leaf at which the model is working. The dependency path of an answer is the lineage of its committed node.

sections.heading: Applying a step.
sections.text: On this tree, the engine applies a step by resolving the node its payload refers to, r ⁡ ( x t ) ∈ 𝒯 t − 1 r(x_{t})\in\mathcal{T}_{t-1} , and applies the operation’s effect (Table 2 ). A Derive resolves to the node its content depends on, or to the current leaf when it names none; every other operation resolves to the node holding its payload (procedure in Appendix F.1 ). A Verify or Restate records the claim beside what the node holds, so that a claim the state contradicts stays visible to the detectors.

sections.heading: Oracles.
sections.text: On the solution state of each node, the engine also evaluates three oracles , task-specific predicates computed from that state and the task definition: sound ⁡ ( v , f ) \mathrm{sound}(v,f) , whether a derived fact f f follows from s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) and the problem’s rules; viable ⁡ ( v ) \mathrm{viable}(v) , whether a correct complete solution is still reachable from v v (the puzzle’s unique solution; the arithmetic over the remaining tiles; a planner run from s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) ), a node that is not viable being dead ; and accept ⁡ ( a ) \mathrm{accept}(a) , whether a committed answer a a is correct and complete.

sections.heading: 2.3 Failure Detectors
sections.text: With the tree and its oracles in place, the detectors read each step against them. Each row of Table 1 is a predicate R ⁡ ( x t , v , 𝒯 t − 1 ) R(x_{t},\,v,\,\mathcal{T}_{t-1}) on the step, its resolved node v = r ⁡ ( x t ) v=r(x_{t}) and the tree before it, and a step on which the predicate holds is an event of that row. In the tree’s terms, a hypothesis of Table 1 is a branch, the established results are the solution state s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) , and a solution is reachable when viable ⁡ ( v ) \mathrm{viable}(v) holds. The three failure modes differ in what the predicate tests. Repetition rows test whether a node in 𝒯 t − 1 \mathcal{T}_{t-1} already holds what the step produces, and which such node: one worked away from, one closed, one already verified, or a subgoal already posted. Underthinking rows test viable ⁡ ( v ) \mathrm{viable}(v) on the node the step leaves, so a switch away from a dead node is justified and fires no row, or whether v v already holds an accepted solution (the literature’s overthinking, filed here because the step leaves a finished solution). Unsupported-deduction rows test the step against the oracles: sound \mathrm{sound} on a derivation, viable \mathrm{viable} on a pruned branch, accept \mathrm{accept} on a committed answer, and the recorded verdict of a verification against s ⁡ ( v ) s(v) . The validation of the engine and the detectors is in Appendix F.2 .

sections.heading: Tasks.
sections.text: We use three reasoning tasks with distinct reasoning structures: ZebraLogic ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , constraint satisfaction; the 24 Game 2 2 2 nlile/24-game , search over arithmetic compositions; and PlanBench ( Valmeekam et al., 2023 ) , sequential action planning under preconditions (Details in Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Models and sampling.
sections.text: We study the Qwen3 family; all results are on trajectories of Qwen3-8B , and the comparison across model sizes is in Appendix C . We sample each question three times, with a budget of 8,192 generated tokens on ZebraLogic and the 24 Game and 16,000 on PlanBench.

sections.heading: Tree shapes and failure patterns.
sections.text: Read off Arbor ’s trees, a ZebraLogic trajectory is one deep chain of derivations split at a few case assumptions, a 24 Game trajectory is a shallow fan of alternative compositions tried in turn from the same start, and a PlanBench trajectory is a chain of plan steps that rarely branches (Figure 4 ). Each shape fails in its own way: the ZebraLogic chain is filled with Re-Derivation across its case splits and fails by running out of budget; the 24 Game fan is filled with Redundant Re-Verification and Derive-after-Prune and fails by committing an answer built on an Infeasible Derivation while a correct one stands; the PlanBench chain accumulates infeasible steps that pass their checks and fails as a wrong plan (Tables 17 and 6 ).

For underthinking we also showed the annotators the lineage Arbor tracked, since the text rarely settles whether the abandoned branch was still viable (Appendix G.2 ).

sections.heading: Local signals.
sections.text: We compare Arbor with the local signals the literature uses to detect the same failures: for repetition, the n-gram rule of Pipis et al. (2026) and embedding similarity between adjacent sentence windows (IRD; Zhen et al., 2025 ); for continuing after the answer, post-answer redundancy (ERD; Zhen et al., 2025 ); for underthinking, switch tokens ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ; and for unsupported deduction, a process reward model (PRM, Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B; Zhang et al., 2025c ) and token confidence ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , each flagging a trajectory’s lowest-scored steps. We set each threshold on development trajectories so that the signal flags the same share of tokens as Arbor , which compares precision at equal coverage (Appendix G.1 ).

sections.heading: Experts confirm Arbor and reject the local signals.
sections.text: Four annotators confirm most of Arbor ’s steps and reject most of the local signals’, and Arbor also recovers more of the confirmed steps (Table 3 ). For repetition the two are comparable, because Arbor records part of what the annotators count as repetition as a restatement rather than a re-derivation.

sections.heading: Local signals flag ordinary reasoning.
sections.text: The local signals recover only a small share of Arbor ’s steps in every failure mode (Figure 9(a) ). Most of the steps they do flag are ordinary reasoning, first derivations or verifications and discourse such as “Wait” or “Let me see” (Figure 9(b) ). Moreover, half of the steps that switch tokens flag as underthinking actually leave a branch the oracle had already ruled out, so a penalty on switch tokens would suppress justified backtracking as often as underthinking (Table 14 ). Figure 5: Arbor ’s subtype counts predict the outcome better than all local signals combined. Gain in AUROC for separating incorrect from correct trajectories over a baseline of trajectory length and task (solid line, 0.86), pooled over the three tasks. Error bars: 95% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: Arbor ’s subtype counts separate incorrect from correct trajectories better than all local signals combined.
sections.text: Arbor ’s per-subtype counts separate incorrect from correct trajectories better than any single local signal and better than the five of them together (Figure 5 ), and adding the five local signals to Arbor ’s does not further increase AUROC (per-task and length-normalized results in Appendix G ). This indicates that the local signals only carry a subset of what Arbor encodes.

We use the following measurements in our analysis, detailed below: (1) Self cost : the share of all tokens on the steps that carry the subtype. (2) Extended cost : the share of a trajectory’s tokens spent in the region of the tree that an event of the subtype opens, defined per subtype (for an abandonment, the steps generated outside the abandoned branch until the model returns to it; for an unsupported deduction, the subtree rooted at the offending node), as the median over events. sections.heading: 5.1 Unsupported Deduction
sections.text: Unsupported deduction is the failure mode that costs correctness: the model’s own verification seldom catches a step the state does not support, and the committed answer builds on it. Three of its four subtypes have the largest incorrect odds ratios of any subtype, at small extended cost (Table 4 ). Verification catches an Infeasible Derivation in under a third of cases on every task (Figure 6 a). Infeasible Derivation lies on the dependency path of most wrong answers and few correct ones on every task (Figure 6 b). The exception is False Rejection , which costs tokens rather than correctness: verification wrongly rejects a viable branch, and the model rarely returns to a branch it has rejected. Its incorrect odds ratio is below 1 but its extended cost is 37.5% of the trajectory (Table 4 ). The model returns to a rejected branch far less often than to an abandoned one on every task (Figure 6 c).

sections.heading: 5.2 Underthinking
sections.text: Underthinking costs tokens rather than correctness: the model typically still reaches the answer, whether by returning to the abandoned branch or by an alternative path, and the cost of underthinking is the search expended in between. Branch and Subgoal Abandonment have the two largest extended costs of any subtype with incorrect odds ratios near 1 (Table 4 ). The model returns to the abandoned branch in between a fifth and seven tenths of cases, depending on the task (Figure 6 c). The exception is Post-Answer Attempt , which costs correctness: the model leaves a complete correct solution rather than an unfinished branch, and rarely returns to it. Between a sixth and a third of failing trajectories held a correct solution, and after the attempt most of them commit a wrong answer or run out of budget (Figure 6 d). Its incorrect odds ratio of 0.08 reflects that most such attempts occur in trajectories that end correct (Table 4 ).

sections.heading: 5.3 Repetition
sections.text: Repetition does less harm to the answer than the other two modes and costs few tokens beyond its own steps: the model re-establishes a step it had proposed long before in the trajectory, and the re-establishment adds nothing to what that step had already given. Its subtypes have the largest self costs but the smallest extended costs of any subtype, and incorrect odds ratios below 1 except for Subgoal Churn (Table 4 ). The re-established step lies tens of steps back for every subtype and task (Figure 6 e). A re-verification flips the verdict in under 5% of cases, and later work rarely builds on a Re-Derivation ’s copy (Figure 6 f). The budget that repetition does not consume goes to dead ends: truncated trajectories spend more of their tokens on steps that can no longer reach a correct solution than trajectories that reach an answer do, on every task (Figure 6 g). The exception within repetition is Derive-after-Prune , the one subtype associated with truncation (Table 4 ): the model re-enters a branch that was in fact dead, without re-opening it, in the large majority of cases (Figure 6 h).

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: Section 5 established what each failure costs and how it arises; a mitigation, however, must act before the failure. We therefore ask whether the tree state before a step already tells a failure apart from the steps at which it could have occurred but did not, which we call at-risk steps . For each subtype we take the steps at which it occurred and, as controls, at-risk steps, on which its precondition held, matched on task, operation and position. We describe each step by the tree state and the operations over the preceding steps and train a classifier to separate the two sets on held-out problems, against two baselines, position alone and the previous operation alone (Appendix I ). sections.heading: The tree state is crucial for separating a failure from its at-risk steps.
sections.text: For each subtype, the stable precursor is the set of state features the classifier selects in every refit, stated as a rule in Table 31 . These rules fall into three kinds of state (Table 5 ). The first is branch content , the constraints fixed, assumptions opened and nodes created on the branch; the second is whether the current node has been verified ; the third is recent operations , the last few operation labels. The tree adds information beyond the operation labels and position: a classifier refit on labels and position alone separates the subtypes whose precursor is recent operations as well as the full state does, but falls clearly short on those whose precursor is branch content or the verification of the current node (Table 5 ), and these latter two kinds precede the subtypes that build wrong answers or leave viable work behind. Table 5 reports the 24 Game, where the state separates every modeled subtype well above both baselines; on ZebraLogic and PlanBench the separation is weaker and strong only for Derive-after-Prune and Infeasible Derivation respectively (Table 27 ).

sections.heading: Two routes carry Arbor ’s offline signals into model development.
sections.text: (1) At inference time, we train a lightweight predictor on Arbor ’s labels, a probe on the model’s hidden states or a monitor over the trajectory so far ( Kortukov et al., 2026 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) , which fires when one of the three kinds of state precedes a failure. Its signal gives existing interventions, a verification prompt, a thought-switch penalty or early exit ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ) , a more accurate precondition than the unconditional one they use now; Table 30 lists the condition each intervention gates on. (2) Offline, Arbor ’s labels mark the repetition steps and dead-end subtrees that trajectory compression should remove, the repeated operation that a reinforcement-learning penalty should charge, and the failures by which sample selection should rank trajectories, in place of the token-count and token-importance criteria these methods use today ( Xia et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025a ; Hassid et al., 2025 ) . In both routes the intervention already exists; Arbor supplies the condition for when to act or the label for what to keep.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Arbor , a reasoning-failure attribution framework that maintains the solution state of a reasoning trajectory step by step and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and that state rather than to the step’s text. On three reasoning tasks, we showed that Arbor flags reasoning failures more accurately than local signals and finds the failures they miss. We used Arbor to separate the subtypes of each failure mode, measure their cost in tokens and in correctness, and explain the mechanism by which each arises. We used the tree state Arbor tracks to separate a failure from the at-risk steps at which it did not occur, and found that for the subtypes that cost correctness or viable work only the tree records that state. Finally, we discussed how Arbor ’s labels can gate inference-time interventions and replace length-based criteria in offline trajectory compression, reward shaping and sample selection.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Three limitations bound the scope of our findings. First, we developed and evaluated Arbor on the Qwen3 model family: we tuned the parser’s schemas and retrieved examples to this family’s reasoning style, and established its accuracy only on reference labels drawn from it. Applying the framework to another model family requires re-tuning and re-validating the parser before one can trust the engine’s state, and therefore every downstream count. Second, the engine presupposes a task whose answers are verifiable and whose search space is finite, so that it can represent the state of a branch and decide its viability and the soundness of a step. This confines the present study to tasks of that kind; open-ended reasoning, mathematical proof and agentic workflows, in which the state is not readily parseable and the notion of a viable branch is not well defined, fall outside its scope, and we leave defining engine states for them to future work. Third, the intervention points and the mitigations built on them are untested proposals derived from the pre-state analysis. Whether gating existing mitigations on these states, or training on trajectories curated with Arbor ’s labels, reduces the failures in practice remains open, and we encourage future work to test it.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Arbor labels failures in model-generated reasoning on synthetic puzzle and planning tasks; it processes no personal data and makes no decisions about people. The four expert annotators were NLP researchers who volunteered, judged only model-generated steps, and saw no personal information. The labels are definitions over a tracked state, not ground truth about why a model reasons as it does, so a mitigation trained or gated on them inherits any error of the parser or engine; we report the parser’s accuracy and the engine’s validation so that users can weigh that error. Reducing repetition or switching on the basis of these labels could suppress useful deliberation if applied beyond the tasks on which we validated them, and a monitor built on the labels should not be read as evidence about a model’s reasoning outside those tasks. The environmental cost of this work is the GPU inference for generating and parsing trajectories (§ 2.1 , Appendix B ); the engine and detectors run on a CPU. Parsing adds one LLM call per step, a cost a deployed monitor would also incur.

sections.heading: Use of AI Assistants
sections.text: Large language models are part of the method: a Qwen3 model parses each step (§ 2.1 ), and LLM judges re-labeled the reference trajectories and validated engine decisions under written rules with human adjudication (Appendices E and F.2 ). sections.heading: Local proxies for the three failure modes.
sections.text: Prior work detects repetition as verbatim looping, by the rule that a response loops if some n n -gram recurs at least k k times ( Pipis et al., 2026 ) , or as embedding similarity between nearby sentence windows ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) . It counts overthinking as the solution rounds after the first correct answer ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , and underthinking as the token share spent after the first correct step is abandoned and the frequency of thought-switch tokens ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Erroneous steps are the domain of process supervision, with step labels from human annotation ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , Monte-Carlo rollouts ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ) or hidden-state scores ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , and benchmarks that ask a verifier for the first wrong step ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . All of these signals are defined over the text of a step or of the whole trace, and none records how a step depends on earlier steps.

sections.heading: Structured views of reasoning traces.
sections.text: Trees and graphs over steps first served to generate reasoning under explicit search ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . For analysis, prior work segments a trace at cue words such as wait or alternatively and labels each block by its function, such as execution, reflection or transition ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , or an LLM maps each trace step to a step of an extracted sketch ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , to a successful or failed attempt ( Feng et al., 2026 ) or to a node of a dependency graph ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . A separate strand clusters hidden states into graph nodes that carry no symbolic content ( Minegishi et al., 2025 ) . In each case the structure comes from the wording of a block or from a judge, and it records what a block looks like rather than what it does to the solution state.

sections.heading: Proxies as the basis for interventions.
sections.text: The proxies above directly drive mitigations: training-side compression and selection by solution-round counts, budget forcing or perplexity criteria ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , RL penalties on redundancy or hidden-state scores ( Zhen et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , and decoding-side suppression of switch tokens, repeated chunks or reflection states, early exit, and pruning of review nodes ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Each intervention carries an implicit label, that repeated or post-answer text is useless or that a switch is harmful, which no method checks at the individual step, and the accuracy lost on removing pre-answer redundancy ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) is one sign that the label is too coarse.

sections.heading: B.1 Tasks and datasets
sections.text: We use three tasks with distinct reasoning structures. ZebraLogic ( Lin et al., 2025 ) : constraint satisfaction over a row of houses; we use the 1,000 grid_mode puzzles (25 grid sizes from 2 × 2 2{\times}2 to 6 × 6 6{\times}6 , 40 puzzles each), each with a unique solution. 3 3 3 WildEval/ZebraLogic . 24 Game : search over arithmetic compositions; we use the 1,362 solvable puzzles of the train split (the dataset has no test split). 4 4 4 nlile/24-game . PlanBench ( Valmeekam et al., 2023 ) : sequential action planning under preconditions, one-shot plan generation. 5 5 5 tasksource/planbench , task_1_plan_generation . We generated for the first 1,664 of the benchmark’s 2,270 questions, and every analysis uses that set: Blocksworld 500, Depots 500, Obfuscated-Deceptive Logistics 285, Mystery Blocksworld 179, Mystery Blocksworld-3 100 and Blocksworld-3 100; the set does not cover plain Logistics. All three benchmarks are public and we use them as released, for research.

sections.heading: B.2 Models and generation
sections.text: We study Qwen3 at three sizes — 1.7B, 8B and 32B — in thinking mode; the 8B model is the main corpus and the other two sizes serve the size comparison. We send each question as a single user message through the model’s chat template with thinking enabled, and generate with vLLM at a fixed seed of 42. ZebraLogic and 24 Game use temperature 0.7, top- p p 1.0, n = 3 n=3 samples per question and a maximum of 8,192 generated tokens. PlanBench uses the model’s recommended thinking settings — temperature 0.6, top- p p 0.95, top- k k 20 — and a maximum of 16,000 tokens; we drew eight samples per question at 1.7B and 8B and three at 32B, and use only the first three anywhere. Every model receives the same task-specific prompt templates (Appendix D ). This gives 3,000 ZebraLogic, 4,086 24 Game and 4,992 PlanBench trajectories per model size. We exclude from every number in the main text the 40 questions per task on which we developed the parser and engine (Appendix E.1 ), leaving 2,880, 3,966 and 4,872 trajectories at 8B. The size comparison uses a panel of 90 questions per task, balanced over the 8B outcome (solved in 3, 1–2, or 0 of its samples) and over length, and run at all three sizes. We ran all generation and parsing on NVIDIA RTX A6000, RTX 8000 and A100 GPUs. Qwen3 is released under the Apache-2.0 license.

sections.heading: B.3 Evaluation
sections.text: A deterministic, task-specific rule scores each trajectory on the answer that follows the thinking. A trajectory that reaches the token limit without an answer is truncated ; one whose answer cannot be read in the required format is invalid ; the rest are correct or incorrect. ZebraLogic expects a JSON grid; it is correct when every house’s attributes equal the unique solution. 24 Game expects ANSWER: <expression> ; the expression must use exactly the four given numbers (otherwise invalid) and is correct when it evaluates to 24; NO_SOLUTION is incorrect since every puzzle is solvable. PlanBench expects one action per line ending in [PLAN END] ; we score plan validity — we replay the plan from the initial state, and it is correct when every action is applicable and the goal holds at the end — rather than exact match to the benchmark’s single gold plan, since many valid plans exist (at 8B, 25.6% of trajectories are valid against 15.2% exact matches; at 32B, 57.1% against 27.5%). sections.heading: Appendix C Model size
sections.text: We compare three sizes of the Qwen3 family, 1.7B, 8B and 32B, on the same questions, and ask whether any subtype appears or disappears with scale and how each subtype’s rate changes. Every subtype persists across the three sizes. Scale lowers the rates of three of the four repetition subtypes and of the two unsupported-deduction subtypes that act on a single step. The rates of underthinking and of the two subtypes that commit or judge a whole lineage, which include the subtypes associated with wrong answers, do not fall with scale. Figure 7 and Table 7 give the rates and elasticities on the matched panel (the same 86 / 88 / 80 problems per task at 1.7B, 8B and 32B, one sampling run per size, 258 / 264 / 240 traces per task and size). From 1.7B to 8B, the per-step rates of False Rejection, Infeasible Derivation, Derive-after-Prune, Re-Derivation and Redundant Re-Verification fall; from 8B to 32B only Derive-after-Prune keeps falling. Branch Abandonment, Post-Answer Attempt, Premature Finalization and False Verdict do not change from 1.7B to 8B or from 8B to 32B, and Subgoal Abandonment rises from 1.7B to 8B and then holds. sections.heading: Appendix E Parser: adjudicated reference labels, metric, and development
sections.text: This appendix documents the parser of § 2.1 : how we built the adjudicated reference labels we measure it against, what the tolerant metric counts, how we reached the final configuration, and what we tried and did not adopt. Every number below re-scores stored parser outputs against the frozen reference and is reproducible from the released files.

sections.heading: E.1 Adjudicated reference labels
sections.text: The reference is 40 trajectories per task (120 trajectories, 46,984 steps), drawn from the Qwen3-8B generations by stratified selection over outcome and length. Hand-labeling it was not feasible, and the label scheme could not be fixed in advance, so we built it the way qualitative coding builds a codebook, with model annotators in the loop ( Kim et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) : a stronger model labeled every step, then LLM judges re-labeled it independently from the written rules alone; where two judges agreed the label stood, and we raised every remaining disagreement to a human as a decision card quoting the steps and the candidate rules. We wrote each ruling into the rulebook, applied it corpus-wide by script rather than as an edit to a single step, and re-froze the reference with a content hash after each round. A final audit read every step the parser gets wrong in all five of its samples against the rulebook and found the reference right on 90% of them. Adjudication against explicit rules, rather than inter-annotator agreement, thus decides correctness ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . The 40 trajectories also served as the development set for every choice below; a held-out review on trajectories the development never saw ( Pangakis et al., 2023 ) is in progress, and we report the configuration and the alternatives we tried so that the accuracy is not the best of many undisclosed configurations ( Baumann et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: E.2 Labeling protocol
sections.text: The parser is one open-weight model, Qwen3.8-27B, with constrained JSON output. It labels steps in groups of fifteen and sees the fifteen preceding steps with the labels it gave them, a few labeled reference steps retrieved from other trajectories of the same task, and the schema elements that each step’s words name. It never sees a summary of the solution state; what has been concluded is the engine’s job, so a label depends only on the sentence and its neighborhood. We take five independent samples per trajectory and decide each step’s label by majority vote.

sections.heading: E.3 What the tolerant metric counts
sections.text: We compute three metrics per step over the steps of the 40 traces that carry a reference label, excluding the few steps whose reference is itself contested.

sections.heading: Strict.
sections.text: The parser’s label equals the reference label.

sections.heading: Tolerant.
sections.text: Strict, or the pair of labels is one that the rulings declared indistinguishable for the engine and the payloads agree on the facts or the action they name. The pairs are: • a fact stated as a fresh inference ( Derive /floating) versus restated from the givens ( Restate ) versus reported as holding ( Verify , outcome hold), when both payloads name the same fact — the engine attaches the same fact to the same node either way; • a plan step adopted ( Assume ) versus echoed ( Restate ) when both name the same action; the echo test looks back over the whole current attempt, which a windowed parser cannot see; • a bare applicability verdict read as enabling an action ( Derive /action-enabled) versus as a check that holds ( Verify ) on the same action; • a plan step under a visible answer header read as confirmed ( Confirm ) versus recapped ( Restate ), and any step label when the header lies outside the parser’s window; • a bare closer (“Yes.”, “So no.”, “Met.”) read as narration ( Meta ) versus as a payload-free check ( Verify ), and a Verify whose only content was an anchor the step does not name. Each pair encodes a ruling that the distinction either does not change what the engine does with the step or rests on context no step-local parser has; strict accuracy penalizes exactly these distinctions, which the reference itself resolves inconsistently across traces. Tolerant accuracy therefore measures whether the parser produced the label the engine needs.

sections.heading: Payload ( Key ).
sections.text: On steps whose reference payload carries schema atoms, the set of atoms the parser emits equals the set the reference carries: the role (kind or target), the facts with their polarity and arguments, the actions with their arguments, and the outcome. An anchor the step does not itself name (an action a subgoal serves, a step a check is about) is excluded from both sides, since it can only come from context. Cited premises are support, not key content.

sections.heading: E.4 Development against the frozen reference
sections.text: We ran every candidate change as five independent samples on the frozen reference (sample standard deviation 0.001–0.002 tolerant), scored it locally, and adopted it only when it beat the previous configuration by at least 0.3 points on every sample. We edited prompts only through builders that record each change, and we never edited the reference to match a parser. Table 11 gives the cumulative result. PlanBench shows own labels and examples as two steps (0.855, 0.889); for ZebraLogic and 24 Game the two were introduced together. We kept step facts where they added at least 0.3 points.

sections.heading: What helped and what did not.
sections.text: Four changes raised tolerant accuracy on the frozen PlanBench reference and we kept them: retrieved labeled examples from the same task, leave-one-trace-out (+3.3 points); own-label context on the preceding steps (+0.6); step facts inline with worked exemplars (+0.4, kept for PlanBench and ZebraLogic, dropped for the 24 Game, whose examples already evaluate every expression); and the reference audit with its rulings (+1.0). Prompt cleaning over four rounds moved accuracy by 0.0 to +0.3 per round and we kept it where neutral or positive. Five changes did not help and we did not adopt them: more examples per group (+0.16), examples oversampled toward Verify and Confirm (+0.0), step facts as a separate block ( − 0.05 -0.05 , strict − 1.3 -1.3 ), the labels of the following 15 steps ( − 0.4 -0.4 ), and a second pass that lists every fact a step states ( Key − 3.0 -3.0 , since it adds cited premises the payload policy excludes). An ensemble of four configurations with 16 samples gained +1.0 over the best single vote; we report it but did not ship it, since it is not a single configuration.

sections.heading: Retrieval details.
sections.text: The example pool is the reference itself. We index each reference step by TF-IDF over word unigrams and bigrams with entity names and numbers replaced by placeholders, so that “So red is clear now” and “So blue is clear now” coincide. For each 15-step group we retrieve the nearest reference step to each current step from the same surface-form family (PlanBench domains with shared operators; ZebraLogic and 24 Game each one family) and from other traces only, then deduplicate and cap the set at 12 examples and 9,000 characters. An example shows the two reference steps before it with their labels, the step, and its reference output in the prompt’s own format. The gain by similarity of the retrieved example was − 3.8 -3.8 , − 4.4 -4.4 , and − 4.0 -4.0 points of error rate for near-verbatim ( ≥ 0.95 \geq 0.95 cosine), moderate ( 0.70 0.70 – 0.95 0.95 ), and loose ( < 0.70 <0.70 ) matches respectively, and − 0.7 -0.7 for steps that received no example; the parser does not copy a twin’s label. For unlabeled traces the pool is the whole reference.

sections.heading: Step facts.
sections.text: For each step, a string match against the Puzzle Schema lists the entities, predicates, and operators its words name (verb forms and common paraphrases included: “on the table”, “hand is empty”, “unstacking”) and the initial-state or goal facts it re-states with the arguments in the right order; for the 24 Game we find and evaluate every arithmetic expression and mark it when it equals the target or uses exactly the four tiles. On the reference, a PlanBench step with no anchors is Meta 87% of the time and a step with anchors 6%; we append the facts to the step in angle brackets and demonstrate them in the examples.

sections.heading: What remains wrong.
sections.text: On PlanBench, 8.2% of steps are wrong in all five samples of the final configuration, concentrated in four confusions — a grounded inference read as narration ( Derive → \to Meta ), a restated given read as narration or as fresh inference, and a need read as adoption — that did not respond to more rules, more examples, or more step-local information. ZebraLogic’s plateau is the echo test (restated cell versus fresh inference); 24 Game’s is narration versus check. We did not train the parser or use a larger parser model.

sections.heading: F.1 Resolution procedure
sections.text: Every mutation of § 2.2 first decides which node the step is about, by one procedure: 1. the engine prefers an explicit anchor in the step (a named cell, expression or action); 2. otherwise it draws candidates from a bounded scope around the current step and the node the model is attending to; 3. it ranks candidates by how much of their content the step already matches; 4. it filters out candidates whose state is incompatible with the step; 5. it breaks remaining ties canonically, and revives a closed node when the model returns to it. Two cursors support the scope: the node the model is attending to and the node it last changed.

sections.heading: F.2 Validating the engine and the detectors
sections.text: Two further conventions apply. We grade a False Verdict (R11) against what the model had written down, not against the truth, which separates a wrong verdict from a wrong premise. Rows are not disjoint; a detector emits every exclusion it makes beside the row with its reason. A replay of the corpus makes on the order of 10 4 10^{4} tree decisions per task, far more than a human can inspect. We validated the engine the same way as the parser. On the 40 reference trajectories per task, LLM judges re-derived the decision for sampled steps from the raw text alone, without sight of the engine’s state. Every disagreement with the engine went to a human as a decision card and received a written ruling. An append-only ledger keeps the rulings; we replay every engine change against it before it ships, so the oracle only grows. We validated the failure detectors on the same trajectories by reading every fired and every excluded event of each row against its definition; the human-annotation study of § 4 measures their precision on the full corpus.

sections.heading: F.3 Worked examples
sections.text: The examples below are verbatim steps from the working corpus, reproduced with their engine treatment; they illustrate the resolution principle of § 2.2 . We identify puzzle instances by trace id; tiles and target are as stated in the source puzzle.

sections.heading: Extending the current line.
sections.text: Trace que352_com0 (tiles { 2 , 2 , 3 , 3 } \{2,2,3,3\} , target 24) has already opened, among other options, a plan for 24 = 3 × 8 24=3\times 8 with an open operand goal “make 8.” Step #9 — ‘‘Maybe if I can make 8 and then multiply by 3?’’ resolves against that existing operand goal rather than opening a new option. The decomposition it names is already a sibling in the tree, so the engine edits that node in place and creates no new node.

sections.heading: Branching into new candidates.
sections.text: Earlier in the same trace, step #5 — ‘‘For example, 3*8, 4*6, 12+12, etc.’’ proposes three unrelated decompositions of 24 in one step. The engine resolves each independently and creates its own option node with its own operand children, all as alternative children of the root — one parsed step, three tree mutations.

sections.heading: Repetition resolved by state.
sections.text: Step #50 of the same trace proposes and immediately rejects ( 3 × 2 ) × ( 3 + 2 ) = 6 × 5 = 30 ≠ 24 (3\times 2)\times(3+2)=6\times 5=30\neq 24 , which the engine creates and closes as a rejected exploration node. Three steps later, step #53 — ‘‘How about (2 * 3) * (2 + 3) = 6 * 5 = 30.’’ is a different string but the identical computation, evaluated in the identical context (unattached exploration at the root, no goal on either occasion). The engine resolves it to the already-closed node from step #50 and records a repetition event rather than a new node; state drives the decision. The converse holds by the same rule: had the second occurrence arisen under a different goal context, the identical computation would be legitimate independent reuse, with no change in the surface text. This is our central claim: grounding to lineage and state separates true repetition from superficially similar but substantively different reasoning.

sections.heading: Fresh start after a reframing.
sections.text: Trace que1060_com2 has an open, previously-worked quest to make 44 / 3 44/3 from tiles { 4 , 9 } \{4,9\} . At step #82, after intervening steps ‘‘Another angle: let’s think about fractions’’ and ‘‘Suppose I take 9 and 4,’’ the model writes ‘‘9*4=36.’’ Although the tiles match the open quest, the engine rules this a fresh start under the root rather than an attempt at the earlier quest. An explicit reframing (a new-approach marker) lies between the quest’s last activity and this step, and a quest hosts new content by context only while it remains the most recent framing.

sections.heading: G.1 Matched-yield tuning
sections.text: We tune each local measure on a development split of 42 traces per task, disjoint from the test traces and distinct from the 40 development questions excluded from the main text, and score it on the remaining test split. The similarity threshold τ ∗ \tau^{\ast} is the value whose flagged token share on the development traces is closest to the token share of our repetition rows (R1–R4) on the same traces: τ ∗ = 0.934 \tau^{\ast}=0.934 on ZebraLogic (777 adjacent development windows), 0.911 0.911 on Game of 24 (817 windows) and 0.956 0.956 on PlanBench (758 windows); the measure flags a window of sentences as redundant when the cosine similarity of its embedding to the preceding window exceeds the threshold. The two step scorers take the bottom- k k share of steps that matches the token share of our unsupported-deduction rows: k = 0.010 k=0.010 / 0.035 0.035 (process reward model / token confidence) on ZebraLogic, 0.015 0.015 / 0.035 0.035 on Game of 24 and 0.02 0.02 / 0.06 0.06 on PlanBench, so the process reward model flags the lowest-scored 1 to 2% of a trajectory’s steps and token confidence the 3.5 to 6% of steps with the lowest mean token log-probability; as trajectory scores for outcome prediction both use the mean over the worst 10% of steps. The n n -gram rule scores a trajectory by the maximum number of times any 30-token n n -gram recurs; run at its published setting (30, 20) it flags one Game of 24 trace, no ZebraLogic trace and two PlanBench traces, and relaxed to ( 5 , k ) (5,k) it selects 49% first work and 48% discourse with a repetition enrichment of 0.70, 0.00 and 1.61 per task. The similarity scores reproduce the reference implementation to six decimals on three traces spanning Game of 24 and PlanBench.

sections.heading: H.1 Tree shapes
sections.text: Figure 4 (§ 5 ) gives the schematic tree of a typical failing trajectory per task. A ZebraLogic trajectory is one deep chain of consecutive derivations (a maximum depth of 23 for the median trajectory) that switches lines of reasoning only about every 40 steps, split at a few case assumptions whose rejected cases are pruned; a 24 Game trajectory is a shallow fan (maximum depth 7) whose nodes are mostly siblings, alternative compositions tried in turn from the same starting point, with a switch between them every 7 steps; a PlanBench trajectory is a single chain of moderate depth (maximum depth 16) that appends one plan step after another and rarely branches, but 1/4 of its nodes are states the model assumes rather than derives, and what it checks are the preconditions each step needs.

sections.heading: Premature Finalization.
sections.text: Of the 915 premature commits on the 24 Game, 66% rest on a lineage containing an Infeasible Derivation, 43% one fired within the previous ten steps, 78% on a lineage the oracle marks non-viable and 75% on a lineage with an unverified node; 67% had passed a check on the committed node itself; 9% rest on nothing a row names, mostly commits of an unattached root. On ZebraLogic 44% of 92 premature commits and on PlanBench 38% of 76 rest on a lineage containing an Infeasible Derivation. When the model later revises such a commit, it does so by committing again, and a failed check precedes the revision in only 7% of cases.

sections.heading: Derive-after-Prune.
sections.text: When the prune was right, the rebuilt node reaches the committed answer in 1.1% of events on ZebraLogic, 0.5% on the 24 Game and 14.9% on PlanBench; when it was wrong, an implicit repair of a False Rejection, in 33.4% on ZebraLogic and 2.0% on the 24 Game.

sections.heading: Branch Abandonment.

sections.heading: Opportunity sets and matching.
sections.text: An opportunity step is a step on which the subtype’s precondition holds on the pre-step state (containment of the occurrences is 100% on every analyzed row). We match five controls per occurrence on task, parser label and trajectory tenth, preferring the same trajectory, then the same problem. The features are 639 quantities of the pre-step state and the operation labels over windows of 1 to 20 steps and since the branch start. We screen them by standardized mean difference with Benjamini–Hochberg q = 0.1 q=0.1 , keep the top 60, and fit gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM; at most 300 trees with early stopping on grouped five-fold cross-validation over the development problems, learning rate 0.05, 15 leaves, minimum 20 samples per leaf, 0.8 row and column subsampling, L2 regularization 1.0, class-balanced) with stability selection; cells with 100 to 300 development events use nested cross-validation. We hold out 40 development problems per task and report every AUROC on the remaining problems. Two LLM judges, with a third as tie-break, judged 20 sampled opportunity cards per subtype against the trace text; acceptance 1.00 (Post-Answer Attempt), 0.85 (Derive-after-Prune, Redundant Re-Verification, Subgoal Churn, False Rejection), 0.75 (Branch Abandonment, Infeasible Derivation), 0.70 (False Verdict), 0.60 (Re-Derivation). 13 of 19 cells use a tightened opportunity set (we add a recency condition so that the detector’s own firing quantity differs between occurrences and controls); the six cells on the main set are Re-Derivation on the 24 Game and pooled, Redundant Re-Verification and Branch Abandonment on the 24 Game, Derive-after-Prune on ZebraLogic, and Infeasible Derivation on PlanBench.

sections.heading: Rare subtypes.
sections.text: Seven of the eleven subtypes have enough occurrences for a held-out estimate, the four repetition subtypes, Branch Abandonment, Post-Answer Attempt and Infeasible Derivation (the rare ones in Appendix I ); we model False Rejection on PlanBench, but the estimate is inconclusive, and False Verdict there separates only weakly. We observe every subtype in the taxonomy at least 76 times at 8B. Five task-rows fall below 10% prevalence (ZebraLogic Post-Answer Attempt 8.4% and Premature Finalization 3.2%; PlanBench Subgoal Abandonment 4.5%, Post-Answer Attempt 7.5% and Premature Finalization 1.6%); all five are present at 32B and, except PlanBench Premature Finalization, at 1.7B. Three are rare because the model rarely takes a common opportunity (ZebraLogic Post-Answer Attempt: the opportunity holds in 72% of trajectories and is taken at 0.0022 per step; PlanBench Subgoal Abandonment 99.8% and 0.0003; PlanBench Post-Answer Attempt 34% and 0.0023), one because a commit run before the answer is itself uncommon and then rarely invalid (ZebraLogic Premature Finalization: 69% of trajectories, 0.030), and PlanBench Premature Finalization is the inverse on a lower-bound count (an in-reasoning commit run in 1.9% of trajectories, invalid in 75% of them). sections.heading: Pre-states by subtype.
sections.text: The pre-states behind the three points of § 6 are these. An Infeasible Derivation violates a constraint the model itself fixed within the previous ten steps in about 3/4 of cases, on the 24 Game on a branch where it has stopped restating what remains, and the derivation is then left unverified in about half of cases and usually passed by the first verification that reaches it. A Branch Abandonment leaves on a derivation rather than a verification, from a frontier leaf with nothing tried under it and no verdict on it; a Post-Answer Attempt leaves a solution’s branch after a run with no verification of the solution. A Redundant Re-Verification re-verifies a node already verified several times, shortly after another verification of it; a Re-Derivation comes when the branch has produced no derivation and no new node in its last three steps; a Derive-after-Prune comes inside a branch still closed, on the 24 Game after a long run since the branch’s last verification or assumption and on ZebraLogic with no prune in the last ten steps; Subgoal Churn follows switching without pruning. These states tell apart siblings of one failure mode: a stalled branch before a Re-Derivation against a long run since the last prune before a Derive-after-Prune, and a young frontier leaf before a Branch Abandonment against a solution left unverified before a Post-Answer Attempt.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22717v1 [cs.CL] 15 Oct 2026 Arbor : Locating Reasoning Failures in Long Chains of Thought through Reasoning State Tracking Huihan Li Affiliation: University of Southern California Siyuan Wang Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong Naga Vamsi Ramana Dinavahi Affiliation: University of Southern California Xiaohui Liu Affiliation: New York University {huihanl,xiangren}@usc.edu , siyuanwang@cuhk.edu.hk Xiang Ren Affiliation: University of Southern California Abstract Large reasoning models solve complex problems through long chains of thought, in which prior work has documented failure modes such as overthinking, underthinking, and unsupported deductions. Existing methods detect these failures from local signals: textual similarity to nearby steps, switch tokens, or an LLM’s judgment of a step’s correctness. However, what a step contributes to the solution depends on the state that earlier steps have established, so identifying failures requires a global view that tracks that state across the trajectory. Therefore, we propose Arbor , a reasoning-failure attribution framework that represents each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states , built as each step creates, verifies, prunes, or revisits a state, and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and the state preceding it. Using Arbor , we refine the three failure modes into distinct subtypes that harm reasoning through different mechanisms and at different costs. We find that the tree state Arbor maintains before a step separates failure steps from the at-risk steps at which the failure did not occur. We discuss how Arbor integrates with existing mitigations at inference time and in training data. Code, data and interactive examples are available at https://inklab.usc.edu/ARBOR . 1 Introduction Large reasoning models (LRMs) solve complex reasoning tasks with long chains of thought (CoT) in which they derive intermediate results, verify them, backtrack and pivot to alternatives. Prior work has documented recurring failure modes in these trajectories: overthinking, in which the model re-reasons about results it has already established ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Pipis et al., 2026 ) ; underthinking, in which it abandons a line of reasoning that could still succeed, a premature switch as opposed to a justified switch away from a line already ruled out ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ; and unsupported deductions, steps the preceding context does not entail ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ) . These failures waste inference budget and some produce wrong answers; reducing them requires knowing which steps fail and why . Existing methods detect these failures with signals that are local to a step: recurring n n -grams or embedding similarity between nearby sentences for repetition ( Pipis et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zhen et al., 2025 ) , thought-switch tokens such as alternatively for underthinking ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , process reward models and LLM judges for step correctness ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and block-level functional labels spanning many steps ( Marjanović et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025b ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Bogdan et al., 2025 ) . None conditions a step’s label on which earlier steps it depends on and what they established, although that context is what makes a derivation a repetition, a switch premature or a deduction unsupported (related work in Appendix A ). Figure 1: How a step relates to the states already established defines a reasoning failure. (a) An excerpt of a Qwen3-8B trajectory on a ZebraLogic puzzle; numbers are step indices, and colored steps are labeled by function. (b) Its tree of reasoning states: nodes are intermediate states, tagged with the steps that created or revisited them, edges link each state to the states derived from it, and the case split at step 66 opens two branches. Steps 87–88 are a repetition : they re-derive the state of step 68 in new words. Step 86 is underthinking : it abandons Case 2 while that branch is still viable. Step 90 is an unsupported deduction : it contradicts the Case 1 assumption. Step 113 is a justified switch : it follows the pruning of Case 1 at step 112. Figure 2: Local signals miss or misattribute the failures that the reasoning state identifies. Columns are steps of the trajectory in Figure 1 . For each failure mode, local signals (gray, dotted) are compared with Arbor (colored, solid), whose arrow points to the earlier step whose state determines the label. Repetition: step 88 shares no n n -gram with step 68, and embedding similarity links it to the clue recap at step 53 rather than to the state it re-derives. Underthinking: a switch token fires at both step 86 and step 113, but only step 86 leaves a viable branch. Unsupported deduction: the process reward model misses step 90, which violates the Case 1 assumption of step 66, and flags the correct retraction at step 112 instead. We therefore define reasoning failures relative to the state of the reasoning , the intermediate results established, the branches open and the constraints in force when a step occurs. We represent each trajectory as a tree of reasoning states (Figure 1 ), in which nodes are intermediate results, each edge records the node a step derives from, and where a step attaches identifies a failure; Figure 2 shows why local signals fail on the same trajectory. We make these relations explicit with Arbor ( A ttributing R easoning failures B y O perations on R easoning-state trees), a pipeline in three stages (Figure 3 ; § 2 ): an LLM parses each step into an operation on a canonical, wording-invariant payload; a deterministic engine resolves the step against the tree built so far and applies the corresponding mutation; and we define failures as relations between a step and a specific earlier state, which refines the three failure modes into distinct subtypes (Table 1 ). We instantiate the framework on three reasoning tasks with distinct reasoning structures, constraint satisfaction (ZebraLogic; Lin et al., 2025 ), search over arithmetic compositions (24 Game 1 1 1 nlile/24-game ) and sequential action planning under preconditions (PlanBench; Valmeekam et al., 2023 ), and report three findings. First, Arbor flags failures more accurately than local signals (§ 4 ). The local signals recover only a small share of the steps Arbor flags, and what they flag instead is mostly ordinary reasoning. Arbor ’s per-subtype counts separate incorrect from correct trajectories better than all local signals combined. Second, the distinct subtypes of each failure mode differ in cost and mechanism (§ 5 ). Unsupported deduction costs correctness, since the model’s verification seldom catches a step the state does not support, and the step enters the answer. Underthinking costs the search expended before the model reaches the answer by another path or by returning to the branch, rather than correctness, since it usually still reaches it. Repetition does the least harm to the answer and costs few tokens beyond its own steps, since the model re-establishes a step it proposed long before and gains nothing from it. Within each mode, the subtypes differ in which of these costs they carry. Third, the tree state before a step separates each modeled subtype from the at-risk steps at which it did not end up occurring (§ 6 ). The precursor of each modeled subtype is the content of the branch, whether the current node has been verified, or the recent operations. Operation labels alone recover only the last kind, and the first two precede the subtypes that cost correctness or viable work, which therefore require the tree. To our knowledge, Arbor is the first reasoning-failure attribution framework that maintains the solution state of a reasoning trajectory step by step and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and that state, rather than to the step’s text. Tracking the state enables us to separate the subtypes of a failure mode, measure what each costs in tokens and in correctness, and identify the state that precedes a failure. We discuss how Arbor integrates with existing mitigation at inference time and in training data (§ 6 ). 2 Methodology Figure 3: Arbor ’s three-stage framework. An LLM parses each step into a canonical operation, then a deterministic engine replays it against the accumulated reasoning state, and deterministic rules map the resulting state relations to functional labels. R4 Subgoal Churn posts a subgoal again after working on others, without progress on it. Q1 : How does it harm reasoning, in token cost, in answer correctness, or both? Q2 : What mechanism lets it arise or persist? We use the following measurements in our analysis, detailed below: (1) Self cost : the share of all tokens on the steps that carry the subtype. (2) Extended cost : the share of a trajectory’s tokens spent in the region of the tree that an event of the subtype opens, defined per subtype (for an abandonment, the steps generated outside the abandoned branch until the model returns to it; for an unsupported deduction, the subtree rooted at the offending node), as the median over events. (3) Incorrect and truncation odds ratios : how much likelier a trajectory containing the subtype is to end incorrect rather than correct, or truncated rather than completed, than a trajectory of the same length on the same task. The main text reports only the values that characterize each subtype; Appendix H gives every statistic for every subtype and task. 5.1 Unsupported Deduction Unsupported deduction is the failure mode that costs correctness: the model’s own verification seldom catches a step the state does not support, and the committed answer builds on it. Three of its four subtypes have the largest incorrect odds ratios of any subtype, at small extended cost (Table 4 ). Verification catches an Infeasible Derivation in under a third of cases on every task (Figure 6 a). Infeasible Derivation lies on the dependency path of most wrong answers and few correct ones on every task (Figure 6 b). The exception is False Rejection , which costs tokens rather than correctness: verification wrongly rejects a viable branch, and the model rarely returns to a branch it has rejected. Its incorrect odds ratio is below 1 but its extended cost is 37.5% of the trajectory (Table 4 ). The model returns to a rejected branch far less often than to an abandoned one on every task (Figure 6 c). 5.2 Underthinking Underthinking costs tokens rather than correctness: the model typically still reaches the answer, whether by returning to the abandoned branch or by an alternative path, and the cost of underthinking is the search expended in between. Branch and Subgoal Abandonment have the two largest extended costs of any subtype with incorrect odds ratios near 1 (Table 4 ). The model returns to the abandoned branch in between a fifth and seven tenths of cases, depending on the task (Figure 6 c). The exception is Post-Answer Attempt , which costs correctness: the model leaves a complete correct solution rather than an unfinished branch, and rarely returns to it. Between a sixth and a third of failing trajectories held a correct solution, and after the attempt most of them commit a wrong answer or run out of budget (Figure 6 d). Its incorrect odds ratio of 0.08 reflects that most such attempts occur in trajectories that end correct (Table 4 ). 5.3 Repetition Repetition does less harm to the answer than the other two modes and costs few tokens beyond its own steps: the model re-establishes a step it had proposed long before in the trajectory, and the re-establishment adds nothing to what that step had already given. Its subtypes have the largest self costs but the smallest extended costs of any subtype, and incorrect odds ratios below 1 except for Subgoal Churn (Table 4 ). The re-established step lies tens of steps back for every subtype and task (Figure 6 e). A re-verification flips the verdict in under 5% of cases, and later work rarely builds on a Re-Derivation ’s copy (Figure 6 f). The budget that repetition does not consume goes to dead ends: truncated trajectories spend more of their tokens on steps that can no longer reach a correct solution than trajectories that reach an answer do, on every task (Figure 6 g). The exception within repetition is Derive-after-Prune , the one subtype associated with truncation (Table 4 ): the model re-enters a branch that was in fact dead, without re-opening it, in the large majority of cases (Figure 6 h). 6 Precursors of Failure in the Tree State Setup. Two routes carry Arbor ’s offline signals into model development. (1) At inference time, we train a lightweight predictor on Arbor ’s labels, a probe on the model’s hidden states or a monitor over the trajectory so far ( Kortukov et al., 2026 ; Baker et al., 2025 ) , which fires when one of the three kinds of state precedes a failure. In both routes the intervention already exists; Arbor supplies the condition for when to act or the label for what to keep. 7 Conclusion We presented Arbor , a reasoning-failure attribution framework that maintains the solution state of a reasoning trajectory step by step and attributes each failure to a relation between a step and that state rather than to the step’s text. On three reasoning tasks, we showed that Arbor flags reasoning failures more accurately than local signals and finds the failures they miss. We used Arbor to separate the subtypes of each failure mode, measure their cost in tokens and in correctness, and explain the mechanism by which each arises. We used the tree state Arbor tracks to separate a failure from the at-risk steps at which it did not occur, and found that for the subtypes that cost correctness or viable work only the tree records that state. Finally, we discussed how Arbor ’s labels can gate inference-time interventions and replace length-based criteria in offline trajectory compression, reward shaping and sample selection. Limitations Three limitations bound the scope of our findings. First, we developed and evaluated Arbor on the Qwen3 model family: we tuned the parser’s schemas and retrieved examples to this family’s reasoning style, and established its accuracy only on reference labels drawn from it. Applying the framework to another model family requires re-tuning and re-validating the parser before one can trust the engine’s state, and therefore every downstream count. Second, the engine presupposes a task whose answers are verifiable and whose search space is finite, so that it can represent the state of a branch and decide its viability and the soundness of a step. This confines the present study to tasks of that kind; open-ended reasoning, mathematical proof and agentic workflows, in which the state is not readily parseable and the notion of a viable branch is not well defined, fall outside its scope, and we leave defining engine states for them to future work. Third, the intervention points and the mitigations built on them are untested proposals derived from the pre-state analysis. Whether gating existing mitigations on these states, or training on trajectories curated with Arbor ’s labels, reduces the failures in practice remains open, and we encourage future work to test it. Ethical Considerations Arbor labels failures in model-generated reasoning on synthetic puzzle and planning tasks; it processes no personal data and makes no decisions about people. The four expert annotators were NLP researchers who volunteered, judged only model-generated steps, and saw no personal information. The labels are definitions over a tracked state, not ground truth about why a model reasons as it does, so a mitigation trained or gated on them inherits any error of the parser or engine; we report the parser’s accuracy and the engine’s validation so that users can weigh that error. Reducing repetition or switching on the basis of these labels could suppress useful deliberation if applied beyond the tasks on which we validated them, and a monitor built on the labels should not be read as evidence about a model’s reasoning outside those tasks. The environmental cost of this work is the GPU inference for generating and parsing trajectories (§ 2.1 , Appendix B ); the engine and detectors run on a CPU. Parsing adds one LLM call per step, a cost a deployed monitor would also incur. Appendix A Related Work Local proxies for the three failure modes. Prior work detects repetition as verbatim looping, by the rule that a response loops if some n n -gram recurs at least k k times ( Pipis et al., 2026 ) , or as embedding similarity between nearby sentence windows ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) . It counts overthinking as the solution rounds after the first correct answer ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , and underthinking as the token share spent after the first correct step is abandoned and the frequency of thought-switch tokens ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Erroneous steps are the domain of process supervision, with step labels from human annotation ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , Monte-Carlo rollouts ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ) or hidden-state scores ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , and benchmarks that ask a verifier for the first wrong step ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . All of these signals are defined over the text of a step or of the whole trace, and none records how a step depends on earlier steps. Structured views of reasoning traces. Trees and graphs over steps first served to generate reasoning under explicit search ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . For analysis, prior work segments a trace at cue words such as wait or alternatively and labels each block by its function, such as execution, reflection or transition ( Chen et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , or an LLM maps each trace step to a step of an extracted sketch ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , to a successful or failed attempt ( Feng et al., 2026 ) or to a node of a dependency graph ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . A separate strand clusters hidden states into graph nodes that carry no symbolic content ( Minegishi et al., 2025 ) . In each case the structure comes from the wording of a block or from a judge, and it records what a block looks like rather than what it does to the solution state. Proxies as the basis for interventions. The proxies above directly drive mitigations: training-side compression and selection by solution-round counts, budget forcing or perplexity criteria ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , RL penalties on redundancy or hidden-state scores ( Zhen et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , and decoding-side suppression of switch tokens, repeated chunks or reflection states, early exit, and pruning of review nodes ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Each intervention carries an implicit label, that repeated or post-answer text is useless or that a switch is harmful, which no method checks at the individual step, and the accuracy lost on removing pre-answer redundancy ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) is one sign that the label is too coarse. A trajectory that reaches the token limit without an answer is truncated ; one whose answer cannot be read in the required format is invalid ; the rest are correct or incorrect.
