Every number below re-scores stored parser outputs against the frozen reference and is reproducible from the released files. E.1 Adjudicated reference labels The reference is 40 trajectories per task (120 trajectories, 46,984 steps), drawn from the Qwen3-8B generations by stratified selection over outcome and length. Hand-labeling it was not feasible, and the label scheme could not be fixed in advance, so we built it the way qualitative coding builds a codebook, with model annotators in the loop ( Kim et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) : a stronger model labeled every step, then LLM judges re-labeled it independently from the written rules alone; where two judges agreed the label stood, and we raised every remaining disagreement to a human as a decision card quoting the steps and the candidate rules. We wrote each ruling into the rulebook, applied it corpus-wide by script rather than as an edit to a single step, and re-froze the reference with a content hash after each round. A final audit read every step the parser gets wrong in all five of its samples against the rulebook and found the reference right on 90% of them. Adjudication against explicit rules, rather than inter-annotator agreement, thus decides correctness ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . The 40 trajectories also served as the development set for every choice below; a held-out review on trajectories the development never saw ( Pangakis et al., 2023 ) is in progress, and we report the configuration and the alternatives we tried so that the accuracy is not the best of many undisclosed configurations ( Baumann et al., 2025 ) . E.2 Labeling protocol The parser is one open-weight model, Qwen3.8-27B, with constrained JSON output. It labels steps in groups of fifteen and sees the fifteen preceding steps with the labels it gave them, a few labeled reference steps retrieved from other trajectories of the same task, and the schema elements that each step’s words name. It never sees a summary of the solution state; what has been concluded is the engine’s job, so a label depends only on the sentence and its neighborhood. We take five independent samples per trajectory and decide each step’s label by majority vote. E.3 What the tolerant metric counts We compute three metrics per step over the steps of the 40 traces that carry a reference label, excluding the few steps whose reference is itself contested. Strict. The parser’s label equals the reference label. Tolerant. Strict, or the pair of labels is one that the rulings declared indistinguishable for the engine and the payloads agree on the facts or the action they name. The pairs are: • a fact stated as a fresh inference ( Derive /floating) versus restated from the givens ( Restate ) versus reported as holding ( Verify , outcome hold), when both payloads name the same fact — the engine attaches the same fact to the same node either way; • a plan step adopted ( Assume ) versus echoed ( Restate ) when both name the same action; the echo test looks back over the whole current attempt, which a windowed parser cannot see; • a bare applicability verdict read as enabling an action ( Derive /action-enabled) versus as a check that holds ( Verify ) on the same action; • a plan step under a visible answer header read as confirmed ( Confirm ) versus recapped ( Restate ), and any step label when the header lies outside the parser’s window; • a bare closer (“Yes.”, “So no.”, “Met.”) read as narration ( Meta ) versus as a payload-free check ( Verify ), and a Verify whose only content was an anchor the step does not name. Each pair encodes a ruling that the distinction either does not change what the engine does with the step or rests on context no step-local parser has; strict accuracy penalizes exactly these distinctions, which the reference itself resolves inconsistently across traces. Tolerant accuracy therefore measures whether the parser produced the label the engine needs. Payload ( Key ). On steps whose reference payload carries schema atoms, the set of atoms the parser emits equals the set the reference carries: the role (kind or target), the facts with their polarity and arguments, the actions with their arguments, and the outcome. An anchor the step does not itself name (an action a subgoal serves, a step a check is about) is excluded from both sides, since it can only come from context. Cited premises are support, not key content.
